entries.title: Germany news: Industry hemorrhaging 15,000 jobs a month
entries.summary: Industry boss Tanja Gönner says the situation is critical but offers opportunity. Meanwhile, politicians head to the Bayreuth Festival and security services warn of racist fight clubs. Follow DW for the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Industry hemorrhaging 15,000 jobs a month

Published July 24, 2026last updated July 25, 2026

Industry boss Tanja Gönner says the situation is critical but offers opportunity. Meanwhile, politicians head to the Bayreuth Festival and security services warn of racist fight clubs. Follow DW for the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The head of the Federation of German Industries (BDI) says the country has become less competitive and called on politicians and business leaders to usher in a course correction

  • The BDI boss urged innovation in the face of Chinese competition and US tariff burdens

  • Politicians including Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Bavarian State Premiere Markus Söder are expected to attend the opening of this year's Bayreuth Festival, the 150th installment of the annual music festival featuring works by 19th century German composer Richard Wagner

  • Germany's BfV domestic intelligence service has warned of the growing threat posed by so-called 'active clubs' as gateways to racist, right-wing indoctrination

Below you can read up on developments from Germany from Friday 24, Saturday 25 and Sunday 26 of July:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Right-wing 'active clubs' spreading in Germany, says domestic intelligence agency

Right-wing 'active clubs' spreading in Germany, says domestic intelligence agency

Germany's Federal Agency for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) is warning of the spread of so-called "active clubs" across the country. 

The warning was published on Saturday in Germany's Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper.

The BfV's own website says such clubs, which got their start in the US, have spread to Germany and other European countries over the past several years.

According to the BfV, the clubs target young white males, functioning as a path from online isolation to personal contact.

The fight groups are seen as a gateway to indoctrination into right-wing extremist ideology and are designed to prepare members for what organizers say is a "coming race war."

The BfV says it is actively monitoring the scene and has recorded the founding of a number of such groups across Germany since early 2024.

Authorities say that they have "information on persons with relevant ties to the scene," adding that they have also seen clear ties between active clubs and right-wing extremist parties.

According to the BfV in the southern state of Bavaria, Patrick Schröder of the right-wing extremist party "The Homeland" (Die Heimat, formerly the neo-Nazi NPD) has been instrumental in fashioning a "roadmap" for establishing a broad network of such white supremacist clubs across the country.

Saturday's Süddeutsche article lists 22 such groups in Germany. Although the BfV has warned of the real world threat the groups pose, it is unclear how many actually exist and function as such in real life as opposed to strictly online.

Skip next section BDI boss says Germany shedding 15,000 jobs a month

BDI boss says Germany shedding 15,000 jobs a month

Welcome back to our coverage.

Tanja Gönner, director general of the Federation of German Industries (BDI) described the fact that the country is losing 15,000 each month "critical" while at the same time arguing that it is not too late to turn the situation around.

Speaking with Germany's dpa news agency, Gönner said: "I am convinced that if we do our homework, we will have every opportunity again. Innovation has long been a top priority for many companies."

Urging investment in artificial intelligence and other new technologies, Gönner said "Germany has lost ground in terms of competitiveness," and therefore political and business leaders should ask themselves one thing with each decision they make: "Does it contribute to competitiveness? Does it help companies become more competitive again?"

Gönner stressed that structural weaknesses coupled with US tariff burdens and Chinese competitiveness had put Germany — a former industrial export powerhouse — in its current position, arguing, "we really ought to be heading to the gym to work off the excess weight we've put on over recent years." 

The roughly 100,000 companies represented by the BDI employ over 8 million workers.

Skip next section We are pausing these updates

We are pausing these updates

Thank you for reading. We will back on Saturday morning to bring you more headlines from Germany.

Bis bald!

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Highs and lows as Bayreuth Festival turns 150

IN DEPTH: Highs and lows as Bayreuth Festival turns 150

The Bayreuth Festival's 150th anniversary, coming up on the last weekend of July, has been clouded by controversy surrounding German-Jewish speaker Michel Friedman. Yet it offers an opportunity to celebrate, including with an AI-enhanced Ring cycle.

Learn more about the celebrations for this year's Bayreuth Festival, which the current chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and his predecessor, Angela Merkel, will both attend, in this report.

Skip next section Foreign Minister Wadephul draws international law and traffic offense analogy in satire show interview

Foreign Minister Wadephul draws international law and traffic offense analogy in satire show interview

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has taken the bold but risky move of appearing in a feature interview on public television's premiere weekly satirical comedy the "heute-show," roughly like the US "Daily Show."

Wadephul speaks at some length to young anchor Fabian Köster in an elevator in a playful interview that's nevertheless focused on entirely serious topics. It spans NATO relations and Donald Trump and Greenland, Russia's war against Ukraine, the low popularity of government he serves in, the war in Iran and Nicolas Maduro's abduction from Venezuela. 

"We're not conducting some kind of foreign policy interview here," Wadephul said at one point with a chuckle after a trickier question, only for Köster to immediately reply "doch!" or roughly "oh, but we are!"

When the topic turned to the US military operation to kidnap Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, Wadephul was asked whether "international law can rub up against the boundaries of Realpolitik." 

"Yes, if you're honest, yes, that's the case," Wadephul said. "But to be honest, we're familiar with this in the rule of law. If you think of yourself in road traffic, for instance, have you always kept to everything 100%?"

Köster said he liked the analogy but noted that "a stop sign is something slightly different" than the abduction of a head of state.

"In the law it's written that you can't drive faster than 50 km/h in a built-up area, but nevertheless sometimes people drive faster. And it's the same, fundamentally, in international law. And you have to deal with that. The laws are there to provide an orientation, but they are never dogmatically upheld 100%," Wadephul said.

Asked whether it was "embarrassing" for Germany to only speak up against breaches of international law if "the right countries" are offenders, Wadephul said it was important to note that there were gradations of color.

"There are differences," he said. "If you, like [Russian President Vladimir] Putin, have been waging five years of war against Ukraine and killing thousands upon thousands of people — including your own people — or if you took this one step against a person in power in Venezuela, who did not exactly keep to international law himself: There really is a difference."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz had faced criticism amid the US operations in both Venezuela and Iran for comments suggesting the situations were "complex." Wadephul expanded on this saying they were politically complex but perhaps simpler from a purely legal perspective, still without explicitly saying they were breaches of the law.

Skip next section Police puzzle over Regensburg bank attacker hitting cashless branch

Police puzzle over Regensburg bank attacker hitting cashless branch

Investigative police officers are trying to nail down the motive of a 20-year-old suspect who was holed up in a Regensburg bank branch for three hours on Thursday and who is suspected of killing an employee.

He is suspected of attacking and fatally wounding a staff member and of attempted robbery.

But Regensburg criminal police investigator Robert Fuchs said the precise motive remained a mystery given the circumstances.

On the one hand, the man was carrying a note suggesting that he was planning a bank robbery and was trying to secure money. On the other, he had targeted a cashless branch, meaning his chances of any meaningful haul were near zero from the outset.

Investigators said in a press conference on Friday that the suspect had used a kitchen knife with a 12-centimeter by 2-centimeter (roughly 4-inch by 3/4-inch) blade.

The 20-year-old was already subject to a weapons ban after a prior incident of him carrying a knife and an electric shock device without authorization.

Police said there were no indications of psychiatric illness but that relevant tests were ongoing. Special units were able to detain him roughly three hours after the first emergency calls. He did not resist.

The man was also in police custody less than 24 hours prior to the crime, investigators said. They said he had turned himself in, saying that he had thrown a beer bottle at a police officer. Police said they investigated the slightly inebriated man's claim and later released him, saying they had no valid reason to detain him.

Fuchs said that the young man had repeatedly come to authorities' attention for minor infractions over the years. He was also repeatedly reported as missing from a facility caring for children and young people.

Skip next section READ — Merz reshuffles Cabinet in aftermath of Spahn's exit

READ — Merz reshuffles Cabinet in aftermath of Spahn's exit

The other big news of Friday morning, frankly, might not live as long in the memory as Klopp's appointment.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has shuffled around some more of his Cabinet posts as he tries to fill the gap left by Jens Spahn's forced resignation amid a surrogacy scandal last week. 

Health Minister Nina Warken is taking up the vacancy running Merz's chancellery after the previous occupant, Thorsten Frei, took up Spahn's job as the parliamentary floor leader for the CDU/CSU group.

Carsten Linnemann will step in for Warken as health minister, and youngster Philipp Amthor will become the junior minister responsible for coordinating with the state governements on behalf of the federal government.

Amthor, still only 33, is best known for a 2020 lobbying scandal that put the brakes on his rapid rise through the party ranks in his late 20s.

Skip next section IN DEPTH — Jürgen Klopp confirmed as new Germany coach

IN DEPTH — Jürgen Klopp confirmed as new Germany coach

In case you missed it this morning, Jürgen Klopp is now officially Germany's men's national team football coach. 

This ends a period of weeks where the deal seemingly needed little more than some dotted i's and crossed t's.

The "Normal One" Klopp takes over from Julian Nagelsmann, who resigned in the aftermath of Germany's disappointing exit on penalties against Paraguay in the World Cup.

DW Sports' Jon Harding looks at a partnership long in the making — with Klopp's name having been linked to the national team job for years already — in this feature story. 

Skip next section Sharp rise in extremist violent crimes in Baden-Württemberg in 2025

Sharp rise in extremist violent crimes in Baden-Württemberg in 2025

The internal intelligence agency, known as the Verfassungsschutz, for the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg has published its annual report for 2025. 

"We all notice that the challenges remain considerable," the president of the state intelligence agency, Beate Bube, said. "The crises of the world are also having an effect here. On top of that there are worrying developments in almost every working area of the Verfassungsschutz."

The report showed rapid increases in violent extremist crime from both the far right, 97 crimes compared to 54 in 2024, and the far left, 49 crimes compared to 34 the previous year.

The number of people classified as far-right extremists hit a new high of 3,790, up from 3,140 in 2024. The number of crimes motivated by far-right ideology dropped marginally, to 2,537 cases.

The number of perceived far-left extremists rose slightly to 2,730, 880 of whom were classed as willing to commit violence. The number of crimes attributed to the far-left scene rose by 80% year-on-year, to 608 cases from 342 in 2024.

The report also noted the growing dangers of hybrid threats, acts of sabotage, online disinformation, and Russian "disposable agents," as well as what it termed the "secular pro-Palestinian extremist spectrum" amid protests in support of Gaza in 2025, differentiating this group from German and Turkish leftists or Islamists.

"2025 has shown us: Extremist threats to our security are becoming more varied, complex and digital," state Interior Minister Manuel Hagel said. "The boundaries between internal and external security, between war and peace are disintegrating. The threats are wholly concrete — and reveal themselves in drone flights over critical infrastructure, in disinformation campaigns and in acts of sabotage."

He said the threats were becoming "more dynamic and subversive," and also noted that they were "reaching ever more young people."

Skip next section VW's Q2 profits dip, boss Blume wants clarity on savings plans by year's end

VW's Q2 profits dip, boss Blume wants clarity on savings plans by year's end

The Volkswagen Group filed its second quarter results on Friday, with profits continuing to dip for the struggling car giant. 

The company logged net profits of €1.54 billion (roughly $1.75 billion) in the second quarter, a 32.9% drop compared to €2.29 billion in the same quarter of 2025.

Although the vagaries of the Trump administration's tariff regime hardly help, most of the company's woes can be traced back to China. 

Sales, particularly of high-value and high-margin models, in the world's second-largest car market are stagnating as China's economic growth slows. And VW is also struggling with intense Chinese competition both on the Chinese market, and increasingly in Europe as well, as Chinese carmakers look to tap new markets amid the domestic slowdown.

Some in the company are calling for more drastic job cuts and factory closures. 

"In a situation where the overall market in China is shrinking by 20% and Chinese competitors are increasing their exports and therefore the competitive pressure in Europe, the currently planned initiatives do not suffice," board member Arno Antlitz said.

CEO Oliver Blume, meanwhile, said a savings program alone would not suffice. He said the priority should be making VW faster, more resilient, more competitive and more innovative. He said they needed to find a way to stay profitable if only selling 8 million vehicles a year, and said he wanted details to be finalized by the end of 2026.

"VW's business model does indeed face pressure in many areas and needs optimization," Blume said, albeit adding that it was also clear that, "a debate about factory closures and historically unprecedented personnel cuts is not the new business model for the VW Group, because that's not a new source of revenue or profits, it brings no technological advantage, creates no competitive products and taps no new markets for our vehicles."

Some initial measures, like reducing the range of products on offer, seeking to streamline production, should be complete this year, Blume said. Larger steps would take time, he added, saying it was unrealistic to expect full factory closures before 2030.

The Volkswagen Group comprises multiple major automakers in Germany and beyond, also including Audi, Porsche, Seat, Skoda, Lamborghini, Bentley and Ducati.

Skip next section Consumer confidence dips slightly as fuel costs rise again

Consumer confidence dips slightly as fuel costs rise again

German consumer confidence looking ahead to August has dipped slightly, according to the NIM index.

The Nuremberg Institution for Market Decisions (NIM) on Friday moved its confidence index down 0.3 points, to negative 29.6 points.

It attributed its latest slight decrease in confidence to lower expected incomes and a higher tendency to save money.

"The ongoing uncertainty is leading to many households remaining reticent when it comes to consumption," NIM expert Rolf Bürkl said. Most people anticipated negative overall economic growth in the coming 12 months, he said. 

It also noted the role of rising fuel costs, particularly diesel and gasoline, after the government's temporary tax relief expired at the beginning of July, only for fighting between the US and Iran to flare up once again.

"Given the expiry of the petrol discount at the end of June, prices at the pumps have risen considerably once again, which is reflected in the price expectations of consumers," the institute said.

The current figures are based on interviews with roughly 2,000 people conducted between July 2 and 13 — which was before the renewed fighting really kicked into gear in the Gulf and started pushing energy prices up at pace.

Skip next section Constitutional Court says Afghan admission pledges cannot be revoked en masse

Constitutional Court says Afghan admission pledges cannot be revoked en masse

Germany's Constitutional Court on Friday ruled in favor of an Afghan woman who filed a lawsuit against the federal Interior Ministry after the German government reneged on the promise to provide protection from the Taliban on human rights grounds. 

The woman was among hundreds of individuals promised admission to Germany in 2021 after the repressive Islamist Taliban returned to power.

In December 2025, Germany's Interior Ministry reversed policy by announcing the blanket cancellation of promised admissions for roughly 640 Afghans whom the prior administration had left stranded in Pakistan for years.

The court on Friday said admissions must be considered on a case-by-case basis, adding, "Even where the executive enjoys a broad measure of discretion, it is never completely free."

Once a person has been informed that they will be granted admission, the court said, individual circumstances must be reviewed before it can be canceled.

The court said the Interior Ministry's decision to simply revoke all admissions was in breach of a German constitutional ban on arbitrary state action.

The case will now be reexamined by Germany's Higher Administrative Court.

The Constitutional Court further ordered the Interior Ministry to continue supporting those Afghans currently in Pakistan until they are admitted to Germany or the ministry reviews their cases in compliance with Germany's Basic Law.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom. Although it's almost the weekend, smack in the middle of what used to be Germany's slowest news season, there is plenty to report.

Beyond the fact that the men's national football team has a new coach and the chancellor is reshuffling his Cabinet, we are keeping an eye on a host of other stories, including a Constitutional Court decision in favor of an Afghan woman who sued the Interior Ministry over its mass cancellation of admissions to the country.

The woman and her two young children were among hundreds of Afghans promised admission to Germany on humanitarian grounds. The court said Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt's 2025 blanket policy reversal was unconstitutional and ordered Berlin to review cases individually.   

Although the German economy has shown signs of life despite prior pessimism, the US war in Iran and resulting price hikes — on top of inflation and the adverse impact of more than four years of war in Ukraine — have again put the crunch on consumer confidence, which is expected to drop in August.

Economic bright spots came from the construction industry, which is apparently booming, as well as unexpectedly rosier sales at luxury sports car manufacturer Porsche. Volkswagen, however, complained that it only netted €1.54 billion ($1.75 billion) in second quarter profits, and says it hopes to have a cost-cutting package figured out by year's end.

If that's not enough, Baden-Württemberg's Interior Ministry registered a "worrying" rise in the number of extremist violent crimes committed in the well-heeled southwestern state, with a growing number of these — from right-wing, left-wing and Islamist fanatics — being carried out by men under the age of 30.

Stay tuned to DW for the latest in Germany news this Friday, July 24, 2026

entries.title: Could 'mesh networks' help overcome authoritarians' internet blocks?
entries.summary: In authoritarian countries, the state is often either monitoring online communications or has the ability to shut them down in a political crisis. But there are other ways that activists can keep in touch.
entries.content:
TechnologyGlobal issues

Could 'mesh networks' help overcome state internet blocks?

July 25, 2026

In authoritarian countries, the state is often either monitoring online communications or has the ability to shut them down in a political crisis. But there are other ways that activists can keep in touch.

Iran, January 2026: During some of the country's largest protests in decades, the Iranian government shut down the internet.

US-based internet monitor, IODA — short for Internet Outage Detection and Analysis — registered almost no data traffic at all and US internet infrastructure analyst Doug Madory described it as "one of the largest government-directed communication shutdowns in history."

During that time, the Iranian government killed and arrested thousands of people but to this day, nobody knows exactly how many. Estimates of the death toll have been anywhere between 7,000 and 40,000, though many observers suspect its closer to the higher number. The lack of clarity is partially because the internet blackout meant that communication with the outside world was all but impossible.

The Iranian government's behavior is not unusual. In Russia, Belarus, Myanmar and Sudan, particularly when governments fear resistance, the internet has become a weapon — because those who cannot communicate cannot organize.

Radio-powered networks

One solution for these sorts of communications crises could be what is known as a "LoRa mesh network."

LoRa, which is short for "long range," is based on a simple principle invented for industrial purposes. Small radio modules, also known as LoRa transmitters, have regularly been embedded into physical silicon chips that are used for industrial devices that connect to the internet, things such as smoke alarms, smart water or power meters and environmental sensors — basically any device that requires long battery life and long-range data transmission but only for small amounts of data.

To transmit information, these devices use license-free radio frequencies of the sort available for civilian use, the same frequencies used by weather stations and garage door openers.

To form an internet-free communications network, users first need to purchase a transmitting device that uses LoRa; these can cost anything from about €30 ($35) to €80 ($91). Then users can connect their phone to the device using special software.

The LoRa devices transmit encrypted data packets over a distance of several kilometers. Each device automatically forwards messages to the next one, like a baton being passed through a crowd. If any single device fails, the message finds the next nearby device, via a different route. This means the communications network that is formed can repair itself.

The result of all of the above is what is known as a "LoRa mesh network."

The different transmitting devices are called "nodes" in the network and because there is no central node, there's no way the communications network can be shut down. The radio modules can be kept hidden and powered either by batteries or a small solar panel.

Only smaller messages, no pictures

The major disadvantage of a network like this is that, unlike the ordinary internet, users can only exchange smaller messages, with a maximum size of around 237 bytes, equivalent to a short text message.

On the other hand, the less data transmitted, the longer the distance it can travel, the less power it consumes, and the less likelihood the radio transmission could be tracked.

Two of the best-known platforms that enable this type of communication are Meshtastic and MeshCore, both of which are free to use and open source.

Both place emphasis on data protection. The transmitting devices merely forward messages and cannot read the content. Third parties, including the police or government agencies, cannot intercept the messages either.

MeshCore's motto is "your communications, your keys, your control."

That the concept works, even under extreme conditions, has been demonstrated by users in Ukraine. Meshtastic-UA offers a real-time network map that shows active nodes throughout the country; there are a lot of nodes near the front lines.

MeshCore has a similar map showing the global distribution of nodes. But there are also many other users who conceal their locations.

It's not possible to censor information sent on LoRa mesh networks. When governments halt the internet, they do things like block internet addresses and domains, scrutinize data packets and legally compel providers to cooperate.

For example, Russian security agencies require locally operating telecommunications companies to grant them direct access to communications data. Those who don't comply lose their license. This works mainly if communication takes place over the internet.

That is something that doesn't happen with LoRa mesh networks. The messages travel via radio waves, bypassing firewalls and surveillance systems.

Mesh networks imperfect

There are still risks to this kind of communication, however. For one thing, transmitters can be tracked as encryption protects the content of a message, but not the sender's location. Authorities with the right equipment can triangulate the radio signals, meaning they can physically locate the transmitter to within a certain distance.

Additionally, in some countries, operating unauthorized radio equipment is a criminal offense. In Iran or Russia, being found to be in possession of such devices can have serious legal consequences.

With any other mesh network — such as those that use mobile phones as transmitters — a LoRa mesh network can only work if enough people participate. If there are not enough nodes, then the distance messages can travel is limited. Building up a network like this takes time, something that isn't possible in crisis situations.

It is unclear whether anti-government activists in authoritarian states are using LoRa mesh networks at all. For good reason, anyone taking part in such a network would prefer not to reveal it.

However Ukraine has demonstrated that the concept can work in the real world. The hardware and required software is freely available worldwide and the technology is mature enough that even people without a lot of technical expertise can set it up themselves .

In a world where more and more governments are using the internet as an instrument of power, and where companies such as Apple are increasingly subject to government pressure, what options are left for safe communication? A network of small radio modules could be the answer for some.

This story was originally published in German.

entries.title: Niger still seeking stability after 3 years of military rule
entries.summary: The military government in Niger promised social, security, and economic improvements when it took power in 2023. Three years down the line, there are mixed reviews on its performance.
entries.content:
Niger

Niger still seeking stability after 3 years of military rule

July 25, 2026

The military government in Niger promised social, security, and economic improvements when it took power in 2023. Three years down the line, there are mixed reviews on its performance.

The military seized power in Niger on July 26, 2023. General Abdourahamane Tchiani , who became head of state, justified the coup by citing the poor security situation, which he said persisted despite international support.

In the weeks that followed, the military government announced a transitional period that was to last a maximum of three years.

However, the political promises made upon taking office have not been fulfilled. The transitional government continues to hold all the reins of power, and the security situation in the Sahel country remains fragile.

In the Tillabery region in southwestern Niger, attacks by jihadists are on the rise. Thousands of people have been forced to flee their villages, plunging the region into a severe humanitarian crisis.

"Today, attacks on the armed forces and the civilian population are significantly more frequent and violent than they were three years ago," Maiga, who lives in the city of Tera, which has a population of 30,000, told DW. Maiga wished to remain anonymous for security reasons.

"Life used to be better despite the insecurity; the weekly markets operated normally and supplies arrived regularly," he said, adding that at the moment entire villages had fled and schools are closed.

The independent conflict monitor ACLED has also said the the security situation has deteriorated since the 2023 coup.

According to the organization, the Tillaberi region remains the main hot spot for clashes between two rival Islamist groups, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin and the so-called Islamic State in the Sahel Province (formerly ISGS). This rivalry has resulted in numerous casualties among soldiers and civilians.

In 2025, nearly 1,200 deaths were recorded in the region. For Heni Nsaibia, a staff member at ACLED, these figures attest to the scale of the security crisis affecting Niger.

The most recent major attack, on July 17, claimed the lives of at least 16 soldiers and 15 terrorists, according to Niger's state media, ANP.

"The situation in Niger has worsened, particularly in the Tillaberi region, where the death toll is the highest in the central Sahel," Nsaibia told DW.

Insecurity taking a toll on civilians

"We live in makeshift shelters and are defenseless against the elements; we take on small odd jobs to survive," a woman told DW.

"I used to be able to live with dignity from my work, but right now it's very difficult; even drinking water is a problem for us," added a local herder.

Young Nigeriens are torn between disappointment and optimism: In the youth assemblies, known as "Fadas," the topic continues to spark discussion. Some — like Fadila — believe that the situation is gradually stabilizing after the turmoil of the first few years.

"For a while, it wasn't easy at all: Salaries weren't paid on time, food supplies… that wasn't easy. But for some time now, things have been going pretty well overall," Fadila told DW.

General Tchiani has emphasized that young people can once again participate in politics. "Before the coup, young people were excluded from decision-making bodies." But in the meantime, he said, an advisory commission has been established that includes young people. "So that means the concerns of young people are now being taken into account in decision-making bodies."

Just two days after the ouster of President Mohamed Bazoumin 2023, junta leader Tchiani announced plans to combat corruption and boost the economy.

But three years later, the people of Niger are no better off, noted Tahirou Garka, a close ally of Bazoum, and spokesperson for the G25, a movement advocating for a return to constitutional order in Niger.

"They have failed economically and socially," he said, referring to the military government. "People are struggling to find drinking water; there is no water, no electricity, no fuel."

However, Hamani Oumarou of LASDEL, a social sciences research institute based in Niamey, takes a different view. According to him, the socioeconomic situation has improved for a large portion of Niger's population, especially for those who are not part of the middle class or the elite.

"Households with low incomes have more money left over to feed their families," Oumarou told DW. However, Niger is also forced to import food at certain times of the year, which leads to a sharp rise in prices.

Rebuilding ties with ECOWAS

Along with Mali and Burkina Faso, Niger is a founding member of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), formed in 2023 after all three countries withdrew from the West African regional organization ECOWAS.

The AES has distanced itself from Western partners and is seeking closer ties with Russia.

Pape Ibrahima Kane, an expert on international organizations, now hopes for a rapprochement between the AES member states and their longtime allies in West Africa.

He sees a positive sign in the fact that former Guinean Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate was elected chief negotiator for ECOWAS a few days ago. According to Kane, Kouyate seems to have been accepted by the AES.

"We are at the beginning of a promising process, as both sides are truly on the same page when it comes to starting talks," he told DW.

For him, economic negotiations should also play a role. Niger depends on access to the port of Benin and on its electricity supply from Nigeria and Benin, both of which are ECOWAS member states.

Reliou Koubakin and Ali Abdou contributed to this article, which was originally written in German.

Correction, July 24, 2026: A previous version of this article stated that Lansana Kouyate is Guinea's current prime minister. This has been corrected.

entries.title: Europe wildfires rage on, forcing 200,000 from homes
entries.summary: Hot, arid weather and strong winds have continued to fuel wildfires in France, Spain and Italy, devastating huge swaths of land and forcing mass evacuations. As national emergencies are declared, the danger remains.
entries.content:
Europe

Europe wildfires rage on, forcing 200,000 from homes

July 25, 2026

Hot, arid weather and strong winds have continued to fuel wildfires in France, Spain and Italy, devastating huge swaths of land and forcing mass evacuations. As national emergencies are declared, the danger remains.

As wildfires continue to engulf massive stretches of western France and central Spain, some 200,000 people have been forced to flee, with flames devouring forests and homes near Bordeaux and Madrid.

Firefighters have said that the blazes, the largest recorded in both countries in recent years, are so massive that they cannot be tackled head on.

On France's Atlantic coast, 44,000 people were removed from the Cap Ferret peninsula, many by boat.

Towns near Bordeaux, the famed winemaking town popular with tourists, were evacuated "as a precaution" as strong winds fueled approaching flames.

On Saturday morning, regional authorities further ordered the evacuation of three of the city's western suburbs "to ensure residents' safety."

In all, French authorities say more than 140,000 people have been evacuated in France's western Gironde and Landes departments.

In Spain, the Interior Ministry said 60,000 have been forced to flee.

EU sending firefighting aircraft to France and Spain

Authorities in France say the country's two main blazes were sparked accidentally, however, as summers become drier and hotter the magnitude of such fires has increased exponentially.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who said the government would do everything possible to protect citizens, warned that a wind shift had transformed the Cap Ferret blaze into "a large, self-sustaining fire that is extremely difficult to bring under control."

"It is now moving east, toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area," added Nunez, who pledged, "We are going to reorganize our response so we can fight it from the ground and prevent it from advancing toward Bordeaux."

French President Emmanuel Macron called for European Union assistance on Friday as well as the mobilization of the French army to halt fires that have so far destroyed 22,000 hectares (54,000 acres) of land.   

The European Commission announced that it is sending three firefighting aircraft to France and four to Spain in an effort to gain the upper hand.

This week's fires have injured dozens of firefighters and killed three of them — two in western France and one in Sicily, Italy, which is now also battling blazes.

Spain declares national emergency

In Spain, the government has declared a national emergency as two of the country's three current fires, all burning near the capital Madrid, merge into one.

Madrid's regional emergency management services said the massive blaze has now reached "its peak and is currently beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain."

The largest active fire in the region, in Guadalajara province, has already laid waste to some 32,000 hectares.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is scheduled to visit affected areas west of the capital on Saturday, as temperatures in the region are expected to top 39 degrees Celsius (102 Fahrenheit).

High winds are also in the forecast, which will make things even more difficult for firefighters.

NASA abandons comms facility amid Spain's summer of fire

The US space agency NASA on Saturday reported that it had been forced to evacuate its Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex (MDSCC), which is located in the region. The facility is one of three worldwide that allow the agency to communicate with spacecraft in distant parts of the galaxy — the others are located in Australia and the US.

"The safety and well being of our personnel is our highest priority and our thoughts are with the families and neighbors who are also experiencing the impact of the wildfires in the surrounding communities," said a statement released by the agency.

Spain, which regularly sees wildfires, has experienced an especially devastating summer. Earlier this month, fires in the south of the country killed 13 people.

Environmental officials say that 1,140 square kilometers (440 square miles) have already been lost to flames this year, more than five times the area burnt throughout the first half of 2025.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Eco wins: Cities, creatures, and tech are saving the day
entries.summary: From an AI-powered cute little pangolin, heat mapping to cool down cities and animals reducing wildfire risks by doing their thing, these real-world climate hacks are helping communities stay ahead of a changing planet.
entries.content:
Nature and EnvironmentGlobal issues

Eco wins: Cities, creatures, and tech are saving the day

July 25, 2026

From an AI-powered cute little pangolin, heat mapping to cool down cities and animals reducing wildfire risks by doing their thing, these real-world climate hacks are helping communities stay ahead of a changing planet.

Nature's own firefighters

Sometimes the best climate solutions have four legs. From goats and sheep in the United States to donkeys in Spain, grazing animals are helping reduce wildfire risk by clearing dry vegetation that can fuel fires.

Carefully managed grazing not only slows the spread of potential wildfires but can also create access paths for emergency crews. It's a simple yet effective example of how working with nature can help communities become more resilient to a changing climate. 

Keeping cities cool: Reclaiming the right to a livable future

Young voices and urban innovators are driving change in the fight against extreme heat. Climate activist Che Chen is taking Taiwan's government to court because he believes access to a livable, cooler environment is a basic human right for his generation and those to come.

At the same time, urban heat expert Tzu-ping Lin is developing practical solutions such as wind corridors, greener buildings and heat mapping to make cities more resilient.

One of the world's most threatened animals speaks up

Conservationists and storytellers are finding new ways to connect people with endangered wildlife in South Africa by helping audiences imagine the world through the eyes of a pangolin.

The cute, AI-powered creature speaks South Africa's 11 official languages, answers questions, reacts realistically and ultimately highlights the threats facing the world's most trafficked mammal, which is poached primarily for its meat and scales.

The initiative is driven by a desire to inspire empathy and action, showing that protecting biodiversity starts with understanding the species we share our planet with.

Edited by: Sarah Steffen

entries.title: India: Cockroaches end protest after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns
entries.summary: India's Cockroach movement says it is ending its protests following talks with the government. That's hours after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan announced his resignation. Follow DW.
entries.content:
India

India: Cockroaches end protest after minister resigns

Published July 25, 2026last updated July 25, 2026

India's Cockroach movement says it is ending its protests following talks with the government. That's hours after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan announced his resignation. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns
  • Cockroach movementends protest in 'good faith' after talks with government
  • Cockroach Janta Party Founder Abhijeet Dipke says diagnosed with typhoid
  • Opposition leaders laud GenZ for 'victory' over Modi government

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Saturday, July 25: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Where did the Cockroach Janta Party come from?

Where did the Cockroach Janta Party come from?

As the NEET-UG controversy was building, so was the accidental Cockroach Janta Party.

That journey began when the Chief Justice of India ridiculed India's youth, likening them to "parasites and cockroaches." The judge has since said his words were taken out of context but it had already struck a cord among India's GenZ.

Abhijeet Dipke, a 30-year-old Indian who recently graduated from Boston University with a master's degree in public relations and political strategy, asked "what if all cockroaches came together?"

He created a satirical party fashioned after the Ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, and millions signed up on its website and social media. Dipke successfully tapped into the frustration of young Indians who have long been facing irregularities in education and lack of job opportunities.

Slowly, both merged and Dipke began speaking out about the NEET-UG controversy. Over a month ago, less than a hundred of Cockroach Janta Party members and supporters began camping at Jantar Mantar in the capital Delhi overnight.

Protests continued but remained modest until Indian activist and educational reformist Sonam Wangchuk joined in to lend his popularity to the cause. He began an indefinite hunger strike.

By the 20th day of the hunger strike, attention on the protest grew. On the 21st day, Wangchuk was "forcefully" moved to a hospital by Delhi police. The visuals of Wangchuk's removal turned the proverbial spark into a fire. 

Hundreds of thousands of young Indians descended on central Delhi in a historical march to Parliament on Monday, July 20, when police eventually deployed tear gas and batons to stop them from reaching the building.

In less than a week, Pradhan resigned, and the movement said it was ending its protest after all its demands have been met.

Skip next section What is the NEET-UG scandal which led to Pradhan's resignation?

What is the NEET-UG scandal which led to Pradhan's resignation?

If you've just heard of the the massive protest movement in India which today led to Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation, let me catch you up on what got the ball rolling. 

In the first week of May, over 2.2 million medical profession aspirants sat for a national medical test across India. That's the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test - Undergraduate, abbreviated NEET-UG.

It is the sole gateway to undergraduate medical courses across India, and millions of aspirants compete for fewer than 150,000 seats, making it one of India's toughest entrance exams.

In the days after the exam, allegations emerged that the question paper had been leaked ahead of the exam, prompting authorities to cancel the test and reschedule a second attempt for June 21.

Between the cancellation and retest, Indian media reported that at least 20 students had taken their own lives due to the daunting thought of having to sit through the high-pressure exam once more.

This was not the first time the NEET-UG or a national exam had been leaked. The incident and related deaths sparked anger among masses and focused attention on other failures within India's education system.

Discourse over corruption, exam manipulation and failure of the Education Ministry have since grown, snowballing into the protest movement which has shaken the country this week, culminating with Pradhan's resignation

Skip next section CJP ends protest in 'good faith' after education minister resigns

CJP ends protest in 'good faith' after education minister resigns

India's Cockroach movement and youth protesters ‌have agreed ⁠to ⁠end their ​demonstration, a spokesperson ​of the Cockroach Janta Party told reporters on Saturday.

"All our demands have been accepted, so we request the protesters to withdraw immediately and return home peacefully," chief CJP spokesperson Saurav Das told reporters.

This comes immediately after ‌talks with ‌the government held post Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.

Skip next section Opposition leaders laud Gen Z victory

Opposition leaders laud Gen Z victory

"Well done to students across the country; we are proud of all of you," Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said in a video message reacting to the education minister's resignation.

"Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation is a huge step towards reshaping our education system," he said, adding they still had to hold accountable those guilty of violence against students.

Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Congress leader and sister to Gandhi, said: "Today is the day an undemocratic and oppressive government was forced to bend to the will of the people of India."

Former Delhi Chief Minister and one of the most vocal Narendra Modi critics, Arvind Kejriwal, congratulated Generation Z for their accomplishment.

"People had lost faith in democracy..the government should understand that they have to listen to the people," he said. "The world bends, all it takes is someone to bend it."

"The resignation of the education minister is an acknowledgment that accountability in a democracy cannot be indefinitely evaded," said opposition leader and Member of Parliament Shashi Tharoor.

"But accountability does not end with a resignation. The deeper failures that brought us here must now be addressed through transparent reforms…" he added.

Skip next section Protesters celebrate Pradhan's resignation at Jantar Mantar

Protesters celebrate Pradhan's resignation at Jantar Mantar

Scenes of jubilation and celebration erupted on phone screens as the Cockroach Janta Party went live from the protest site at Jantar Mantar, following the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Sweat-soaked youths and Cockroach movement leaders jumped in excitement, clapped their hands and threw their fists up in the air. "This is a victory of India's youth," Dipke said, with mic in hand and a wide smile on his face.

Skip next section 'It's a victory of democracy': Sonam Wangchuk

'It's a victory of democracy': Sonam Wangchuk

Activist Sonam Wangchuk celebrated the news of Pradhan's resignation from a hospital in Gurago, where he is still recovering from a 26-day hunger strike.

"IT'S A VICTORY OF DEMOCRACY direct democracy... straight from the streets," he said in a post.

"Congratulations CJP, Gen Z of the nation and thank you all citizens for shedding fear and the fear of fear and rising up from every corner of the nation," he said, adding that it was now time to move from demanding accountability to reforms.

Skip next section 'Remember, do not mess with cockroach': Dipke

'Remember, do not mess with cockroach': Dipke

When Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan broke the news of his resignation in a two-page explanation letter, the Cockroach Janta Party's immediate reaction — at least on social media — was not celebration.

The political pressure group simply posted an "update" on its core demands from the government.

"1.Dharmendra Pradhan must resign - *CHECK*

2. 1 crore to the families of all students who died by suicide - PENDING

3. No action against any of the student protesters - PENDING," the post said.

In a speech addressing protesters at Jantar Mantar, CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke said action must be taken against the police officers who injured women and students by the use of inappropriate and brutal force.

He named certain police officers accused of brutality and said, "if we can make a minister resign, what are you?" he said.

"Remember, do not mess with cockroach," Dipke said, adding: "and to the people of India, this is how a democracy should be."

Also in a moment of humility, Dipke asked supporters not to make him a "hero" because of Pradhan's resignation. "Don't make this mistake...The country has been ruined because of making one person a hero," he said, alluding to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Skip next section Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns

Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns

India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan said he has sent his resignation to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in what is being seen as a major victory for the Cockroach movement and student protesters. 

It was not immediately clear if Modi has or will accept Pradhan's resignation.

"Amid the situation that has emerged in Jantar Mantar and across the country, my resignation has been sent to the Honorable Prime Minister so that anti-national forces do not take advantage of the situation, the unity of the country remains intact, no student in India gets entangled in legal complications, and our children can focus their time on their studies and careers," Pradhan said in a post on X.

"I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations of ​the country's youth," he went on to say.

Cheers erupted among the thousands of protesters who have been rallying in central Delhi and elsewhere as ⁠the ​news spread. The update reached protesters quickly despite suspended internet services in and around the protest site.

This is the second time Modi's government has faced a significant and public setback due to a mass protest.

In 2021, the government was forced to repeal contentious farm sector laws after hundreds of thousands of farmers and union leaders camped at the borders of Delhi. Farmers had argued that the new legislation would leave eat into their income and leave them vulnerable to large corporations. 

Skip next section CJP calls for nationwide candle march on Sunday

CJP calls for nationwide candle march on Sunday

The Cockroach movement has called for a nationwide candle march on Sunday evening, as it looks to keep up the pressure on the Narendra Modi government.

"One person, one candle. For every student the government failed. March together in silence," the poster said.

That is despite ongoing talks between the movement's spokespeople and the government. CJP leaders and protesters on the ground have said that they will keep taking to the streets until Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.

Critics of the movement have pointed out that the government has arrested several reported to be involved in the paper leak scandal. Moreover, paper leaks have long happened in India even under previous governments. A common arguments is that removing a minister would not make a difference.

Countering this, protesters and their supporters have said that as education minister, the buck stops with Pradhan. CJP leaders have repeated that the minister must take accountability for the leak, which reportedly pushed at least 20 students to suicide. 

Skip next section PM Modi 'thanks friends' in another late night video

PM Modi 'thanks friends' in another late night video

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi uploaded yet another reel overnight — this time thanking "friends" for their suggestions over a Gen-Z style video posted late the night before.

"I had a chance to meet you all late last night. The response to the video I posted, the insightful suggestions... thank you everybody," he said in the latest video.

In the previous reel, the prime minister had appealed to the nation that the government had taken several steps to counter the paper leak issue. It was one of his lesser-produced videos shot in a less-than ideal angle, seemingly in an attempt to connect with the youth.

Many protesters on ground read the video as a "desperate attempt" to manage the students' anger as protests began to spread nationwide. "He suddenly woke up and posted a panic reel because they didn't expect the protests to reach this stage," one protesters told DW, asking to stay anonymous over fear of backlash.

Meanwhile, social media did what it does best and made memes.

The Prime Minister appears to have acknowledged that he is watching and learning.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: Overnight scenes from the protest at Jantar Mantar

IN PICTURES: Overnight scenes from the protest at Jantar Mantar

Skip next section CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke diagnosed with typhoid

CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke diagnosed with typhoid

Political pressure group Cockroack Janta Party's leader and Founder Abhijeet Dipke has been diagnosed with typhoid, he said in the early hours of Saturday in a post on X.

"I have been diagnosed with typhoid. My treatment is on, I am being administered IV [fluids] day and night," Dipke said, holding up his hand to show the catheter set up.

"But I really want to thank the cockroaches which have been protesting peacefully across the nation and have made this movement so successful. A big, big thankyou to all and congratulation to you all for such a big,big success. And I am very sure if we continue protesting peacefully, Dharmendra Pradhan will have to resign," he said, speaking of the education minister.

Dipke and several protesters have been camping at the Jantar Mantar protest site since over a month now. 

Skip next section WATCH: Delhi police crack down on student protests

WATCH: Delhi police crack down on student protests

There have been accusations of police brutality in New Delhi after police used tear gas and batons against anti-government protesters from the "Cockroach" movement.

The mood among protesters is rather tense, DW correspondent Adil Bhat reports. People gather in large numbers, chant slogans and demand the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

The current protest movement is not tied to any ideology, he adds: "it will continue even if there is no leadership."

Skip next section Government-CJP second round of talks set for Saturday evening

Government-CJP second round of talks set for Saturday evening

Cockroach Janta Partyspokesperson and Indian government respresentatives are set to meet for the second round of talks on Saturday evening, after first round of talks on Friday did not lead to a breakthrough. 

This comes amid youth-led nationwide protests in India against a struggling education system and Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, after a national medical enterance exam's question papers leaked in May.

The leak affected millions of medical aspirants and is believed to have led to several students committing suicide.

"They had given us the time for 3:30-4:00 p.m. (1000 GMT-1030 GMT) today. The location has not been finalised yet," CJP National Spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka told news agency ANI.

"Discussions are very clear. We should get written confirmation for the two demands on which there has been in-principle agreement. So that they can be closed. We need clarity over Dharmendra Pradhan — whether they will seek his resignation or not. We want an answer in Yes or No because there is not much scope for deliberation over this," he said.

On Friday, CJP's chief spokesperson Saurav Das and Ranka met Union Ministers Jagat Prakash Nadda and Jitender Singh at "neutral ground."

The ministers were presented CJP's three core demands: Pradhan's resignation, monetary compensation for the families of the students who committed suicide and no legal action against peaceful protesters.

The ministers reportedly sought a day's time to respond on the resignation demand and agreed to the other two.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello and welcome to DW's India blog.

This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from the New Delhi bureau and I will be your guide through the massive student-led protests which began in the capital and are now spreading across the nation.

This is a high stakes weekend. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government is set to hold a second round of talks with Cockroack Janta Party spokespeople on Saturday evening.

Remember, yesterday government representatives had asked for a day's time to respond on the movement's central demand — the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Protesters in central Delhi continue to show up in large numbers which are expected to grow even more into the weekend.

Meanwhile, Modi's cabinet approved amendments to a paper leak legislation with stricter punishments and fines for those convicted. The bill could be introduced in the Indian Parliament as soon as Monday.

Tune in for all of this and more.

entries.title: Iran war: Houthis vow response to 'dangerous escalation' by Saudi Arabia
entries.summary: Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claim that civilian sites were targeted in Saudi strikes on the Yemeni port city of Hodeida. Saudi Arabia says it hit military targets. DW has more.
entries.content:
Middle East

Iran war: Houthis vow response to Saudi strikes on Hodeida

Published July 25, 2026last updated July 25, 2026

Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claim that civilian sites were targeted in Saudi strikes on the Yemeni port city of Hodeida. Saudi Arabia says it hit military targets. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Houthi rebels in Yemen say Friday's Saudi strikes on the port city of Hodeida hit civilian infrastructure, injuring two people
  • Saudi Arabia says it will do everything necessary to protect its shipping amid a Houthi-enforced maritime blockade in the Red Sea
  • A flare-up between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, and the consequent disruption of shipping in the Red Sea, could worsen the global economic fallout from the war

Here are the latest developments from the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Saturday, July 25:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section WATCH: US President Trump threatens 'massive attacks' on Iran

WATCH: US President Trump threatens 'massive attacks' on Iran

President Donald Trump says the US and Iran are talking but Tehran is not yet ready for a peace deal. But is the US prepared for the "major military punishment" that Trump has promised Iran?  

Skip next section Air defense system operated by Greek military downs missiles over Saudi Arabia — report

Air defense system operated by Greek military downs missiles over Saudi Arabia — report

An air ‌defense ⁠system ⁠operated ​by Greek military ​personnel in ​Saudi ‌Arabia intercepted ‌two ballistic missiles ‌launched ​from Yemen on Saturday, news agency Reuters cited Greek security sources as saying.

The missiles were targeting oil refineries ⁠in ​Yanbu, Reuters added.

Reuters reported that the interception ⁠was ​the second time that Greek military personnel had operated the system.

Since 2021, an bilateral defense agreement to protect Saudi Arabia's critical energy infrastructure has seen Greece deploy a US-made Patriot air defense battery, operated by Hellenic Air Force personnel.

Earlier in the morning, the Saudi Civil Defense had alerted residents of Yanbu about a "potential danger" in the governorate, without giving any further details. It later advised the public that the said danger had passed.

A series of strikes and counter-strikes by Yemen's Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia have opened a new front in a war that has gripped the Middle East following US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

Skip next section Why Iran's Pickaxe Mountain is a tough target for the US

Why Iran's Pickaxe Mountain is a tough target for the US

A mysterious underground complex near Iran's Natanz nuclear facility is drawing global attention after US President Donald Trump suggested it could become the target of a military strike, with Trump claiming there may be uranium centrifuges located at the site.

Tehran has released almost no information about the complex burrowed under what is known in Farsi as "Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La," or Pickaxe Mountain.

Although the site has surfaced repeatedly in reports over the past few years, its purpose remains unclear. That uncertainty has made it one of the most closely watched locations linked to Iran's nuclear activities.

Read more here.

.

Skip next section WATCH: Is the US prepared for the 'major military punishment' that Trump has promised Iran?

WATCH: Is the US prepared for the 'major military punishment' that Trump has promised Iran?

President Donald Trump says the US and Iran are talking but Tehran is not yet ready for a peace deal. Trump says the US is ‘locked and loaded’ and has threatened to intensify attacks against Iran which it has launched daily since the ceasefire broke down two weeks ago. 

Skip next section Houthis claim missile attack in Saudi Arabia's south

Houthis claim missile attack in Saudi Arabia's south

Yemen's Houthi rebels have claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan.

The Iran-backed group's Ansarollah media posted on Telegram early Saturday that fires had broken out in Jizan after a "Yemeni missile attack."

The militant group had earlier accused US-ally Riyadh of a "dangerous escalation"and warned that its actions "will not go unanswered."

A Saudi Civil defense alert said "danger has passed in Jazan Province," without mentioning a missile strike.

It issued another warning for "potential danger" in the Yanbu governorate.

Skip next section Yemen's Houthis vow retaliation for Saudi strikes

Yemen's Houthis vow retaliation for Saudi strikes

The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have accused Saudi Arabia of targeting civilian infrastructure, amid an escalating flare-up with Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia on Friday hit the Houthi-held port city of Hodeida with strikes, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said, in response to the rebel group attacking Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea as part of a maritime blockade.

"The Saudi enemy's targeting of civilian facilities in Hodeida and Kamaran island constitutes a dangerous escalation," the Houthis' Ansarollah media posted on Telegram.

"We affirm that these recent crimes will not go unanswered."

Houthi-run Al Masirah television said on Saturday that Saudi strikes had targeted facilities belonging to the state telecommunications corporation and Kamaran island, off Yemen's western coast.

The broadcaster reported that one worker was wounded in Hodeida while a woman was also injured on Kamaran Island.

The Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, claimed that it hit "Houthi military sites" and destroyed targets that were posing a threat to commercial vessels in the Red Sea.

Riyadh said it would do everything necessary to protect its ships, warning the Houthis that if they continued "hostile acts then there will be no hesitation in responding."

For Saudi Arabia, a top oil producer, the Red Sea had emerged a critical shipping alternative to the ​war-blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

After the Strait of Hormuz, the conflict has now embroiled another one of the world's vital energy shipping corridors — the Red Sea.

Earlier this week, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced a blockade of Saudi vessels in the Red Sea, and then claimed strikes on two Saudi oil tankers for violating it.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen responded on Friday by attacking the Houthi-held Yemeni port city of Hodeida. The coalition said it had only targeted "military" sites linked to threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea.

But the Houthis accused the coalition of targeting civilian infrastructure and have now said they would retaliate against Saudi Arabia.

Before we dive in further on the deepening crisis in the Middle East, here is a round-up of developments in the region on Friday:

  • The US launched strikes on Iran for the 13th consecutive night. Iranian state media reported explosions across the country
  • US President Donald Trump said Iran will pay the financial cost of any damage to ships or cargo amid the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz
  • Trump also claimed that Tehran is getting "very serious" in its discussions with the US
  • On the other hand, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran would hold any country assisting the US in an attack on the Islamic republic, accountable
  • The Houthi rebel group in Yemen denied that it was completely closing the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean

Stay tuned as we bring you the latest on the US-Iran war and the Middle East.

entries.title: Trump addresses rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner
entries.summary: The event was originally scheduled for April but was disrupted by the alleged attempted assassination of Donald Trump. His hourlong speech combined jokes with attacks on members of the press.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump speaks at delayed White House Correspondents' Dinner

July 25, 2026

The event was originally scheduled for April but was disrupted by the alleged attempted assassination of Donald Trump. His hourlong speech combined jokes with attacks on members of the press.

US President Donald Trump addressed hundreds of journalists at a scaled-down and rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner on Friday night.

The gala was held amid heightened security measures, three months after the original event was cut short by an alleged attempt to assassinate Trump.

Trump delivered the speech at Washington's Waldorf Astoria, a smaller venue that held only about 700 people, instead of its usual venue, the Washington Hilton.

Trump jokes about possible third term

"Just like my presidency, the second time is always better. It's always better," Trump said. "And the third time will be better yet."

"I'm only kidding," he added.

Trump has repeatedly suggested that he would entertain the idea of a third term, despite the 22nd Amendment of the US Constitution barring a president from being elected more than twice.

Trump makes light of shooting incident, praises Secret Service officer

Trump also joked about the incident during April's gala, when a gunman tried to storm a security checkpoint before he was stopped by security personnel before making it into the ballroom where the dinner was being held.

"After hearing the gunshots, many people yelled, 'Get down! Get down!', which caused Nicki Minaj to start twerking. Do you believe it? Get down!" Trump said.

The president also praised Victor Gonzalez, the Secret Service officer who was shot during the April confrontation with the suspect. "What he did was amazing," Trump said. "We salute you and we thank you with all of our hearts."

What else did Trump say during the White House Correspondents' Dinner?

This year's events were the first Trump has attended as president. He did not appear at any correspondents' dinners during his first term.

Trump said he had not attended previous dinners because the press has treated him "unfairly," although he promised to come back next year.

The US president has long had a hostile relationship with many journalists and media outlets .

During his speech, he attacked some journalists, including CNN's Kaitlan Collins — whom Trump repeatedly complained about not smiling enough — and Josh Dawsey of The Wall Street Journal. Both were honored with journalism awards at the gala.

Despite those barbs, Trump ended his speech, which lasted over an hour, by saying that he has "tremendous respect" for the reporters attending the dinner.

"I have tremendous respect for the people in this room. Sometimes I don't feel you treat me fair. Maybe you do. I don't know," Trump said.

Trump vs the media

The Trump administration has filed lawsuits against multiple media outlets, barred the Associated Press from the White House ​press pool and limited journalists' access ‌to the Pentagon, among other measures.

Trump has maintained that the measures aim to improve accountability and address media bias.

Speaking in the Oval Office on Friday, he defended federal subpoenas — which were later withdrawn — issued to New York Times journalists over their reporting on the security of the new Qatari-donated Air Force One.

"We're not after journalists. We're after leakers. We're after people that are cowards, people that are unpatriotic, people that ⁠are treasonous in many cases. And the way ​you find them is through the journalists," Trump said.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Starship completes 1st test flight since SpaceX IPO
entries.summary: Starship splashed down in the Indian Ocean to complete its 13th test flight and its first since Elon Musk's SpaceX went public in June.
entries.content:
July 25, 2026

Starship splashed down in the Indian Ocean to complete its 13th test flight and its first since Elon Musk's SpaceX went public in June.

SpaceX's Starship megarocket completed a test flight on Friday, the first since Elon Musk's company went public on Wall Street in June.

The ship splashed down into the Indian Ocean, which was celebrated by SpaceX employees watching along from the firm's headquarters in Starbase, Texas.

"Starship is intact, floating in the ocean and transmitting telemetry!" Musk said on X.

This was the world's most powerful rocket's 13th flight.

Previous tests had ended with Starship in flames or exploding at splashdown, or breaking up in midair.

What do we know about the latest SpaceX Starship test?

Starship, which is around 122 meters (400 feet) tall, deployed 20 Starlink satellites into suborbital space.

After ​briefly contacting SpaceX's network of around 10,000 orbiting satellites, they reentered Earth's ​atmosphere and burned up as planned.

The hourlong test "will provide critical data as we prepare to expand our Starlink constellation" of the company's satellite internet service, SpaceX said.

By the end of 2026, SpaceX aims to use the Starship rocket to expand its Starlink network with the latest V3 satellites, providing coverage in remote areas where traditional cellular networks are unavailable.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

Iran war: Saudi-led coalition attacks Yemen's Hodeida

Published July 24, 2026last updated July 25, 2026

The strikes come after the Iran-backed Houthis attacked several Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea in recent days. The escalation comes as the US and Iran also vie for control of the vital Strait of Hormuz. DW has more.

Below are the main developments on the US war with Iran and news from the Middle East on Friday, July 24:  

  • Saudi-led coalition strikes the Houthi-held Yemeni port city of Hodeida
  • The attacks come after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed several strikes on Saudi oil tankers as part of itsRed Seablockade
  • The Houthisclaim Bab al-Mandeb Strait is not closed, saying the blockade only targets Saudi ships
  • EU naval mission ASPIDES raises risk level for merchant ships in Red Seadue to Houthi actions
  • This comes as the US and Iranvie for control over theStrait of Hormuz, another key regional passageway for energy exports
  • Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu vows to 'act with full force' after fatal West Bank clashes
  • USconducts strikes on Iran for 13th consecutive night; Iran says IRGC base in northern Iran was attacked
